summary: Virginia has no state law making smoke or carbon monoxide alarms a condition of selling a house; alarms are required through the Uniform Statewide Building Code when a home is built or renovated, and your city or county may require them in existing homes by local ordinance.
alarmType: Where a locality requires alarms in existing dwellings by ordinance, the alarms must be installed only in conformance with the Uniform Statewide Building Code and may be either battery operated or AC powered. The installation cannot be made to require new or additional wiring. A locality also cannot force an upgrade beyond the building code that applied at the time of the building's last permitted renovation.
coAlarms: No statewide requirement tied to sale. In the Code of Virginia titles searched, CO alarms appear only as a tenant duty not to tamper with a CO alarm the landlord installed; there is no seller or homeowner installation mandate. CO alarms in new work come from the Uniform Statewide Building Code.
certification: Nothing at sale. A certificate requirement exists only in the rental context: a local ordinance may require a rental-unit owner to give the tenant a certificate that all smoke alarms are present, inspected, and in good working order, and a landlord must provide such a certificate no more than once every 12 months. The Department of Housing and Community Development publishes the certification form.
citation: Va. Code § 15.2-922 (smoke alarms in certain buildings; local ordinance authority); Uniform Statewide Building Code, Va. Code § 36-97 et seq.; Va. Code §§ 36-99.3, 36-99.4, 36-99.5, 36-99.5:1 (institutional and deaf/hard-of-hearing alarms); Va. Code §§ 55.1-1220, 55.1-1227 and § 36-139.01 (rental smoke alarm certificate and tenant duties)
notVerified: The finding that no sale/transfer requirement exists rests on a full-text search of the Code of Virginia CSV exports for Title 36 (Housing), Title 55.1 (Property and Conveyances, which contains the Residential Property Disclosure Act), Title 27 (Fire Protection), and Title 15.2 (Counties, Cities and Towns), downloaded from https://law.lis.virginia.gov/law-library (files /CSV/CoVTitle_36.csv, CoVTitle_55.1.csv, CoVTitle_27.csv, CoVTitle_15.2.csv). No section in those titles ties a smoke or CO alarm to a sale, transfer, or closing. Other titles were not searched.
The actual number, placement, and power requirements for alarms sit in the Uniform Statewide Building Code regulations (13VAC5-63) rather than the statute; those regulations were not read.
Local ordinances adopted under § 15.2-922 were not checked. A Virginia city or county could impose its own requirement, including at sale.
